questions.explanation: slice takes elements from index 1 up to but not including index 3, which is two elements. The end boundary is exclusive, a common source of off-by-one confusion. Carrying the operation through gives 2; common slips include treating the slice end index as included and treating the start index as the end.
questions.hint: The second argument of slice is not part of the result.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — splice.

options.misconception: Reporting the count of removed items instead
Assuming splice leaves the array unchanged
Removing one item instead of two

questions.explanation: splice removes two elements starting at index 1 and returns them, leaving 3 elements. Unlike slice, splice changes the original array in place. The printed value is 3, while the alternatives come from assuming splice leaves the array unchanged, reporting the count of removed items instead and removing one item instead of two.
questions.hint: splice is destructive: the original array shrinks by the removed count.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — map.

options.misconception: Assuming map returns the original element

questions.explanation: map applies the doubling callback to every element and returns a new array, so the first output is 2396 times two, or 4792. The source array is not changed. Both the direct number 4792 and the equivalent sum 2396 plus 2396 match, whereas 2396 and 2398 come from assuming map returns the original element and adding instead of multiplying.
questions.hint: map builds a new array from each callback result.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — filter.

stimulus.body: A program is processing the value 2397.

options.misconception: Counting rejected items instead of kept ones
Assuming every element passes the test

questions.explanation: filter keeps only values strictly greater than 88; exactly 2 of the three entries qualify. Elements equal to the threshold are rejected by the strict comparison. The printed value is 2, while the alternatives come from assuming every element passes the test, counting rejected items instead of kept ones and applies a different mistaken operation.
questions.hint: Check each element against the strict greater-than test.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — reduce.

answer.exemplar: reduce folds every element into the accumulator starting from zero, producing the sum 2431. The initial value is the seed, not an extra element. The result is 2431.

questions.explanation: reduce folds every element into the accumulator starting from zero, producing the sum 2431. The initial value is the seed, not an extra element. A complete answer names 2431 and justifies it from the code rather than guessing.
questions.hint: The accumulator starts at the supplied initial value.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — foreach.
questions.explanation: forEach calls the callback once per element, adding each to sum, which reaches 2409. forEach returns undefined but the closure updates the outer variable. Carrying the operation through gives 2409; common slips include only the first callback runs in their view and confusing count with accumulated total.
questions.hint: The callback runs once for every array element.
